segments.say: In the late nineteen sixties and early nineteen seventies, at a nursery school on the campus of Stanford University, a psychologist named Walter Mischel and his colleagues ran a series of experiments that would become world famous. The setup was simple. A child, around four or five years old, sat at a table with a treat in front of them.

Often, it was a marshmallow. The researcher explained the choice. You can eat this treat now. Or, if you wait until I come back, you can have two. And if you want to stop waiting at any time, just ring this bell, and I'll come back, and you can have the one treat. Then the researcher left the room.

What happened next has been described many times, and it's quite charming. Some children ate the marshmallow almost immediately. Others waited a little, then gave in. And some managed to wait for a long time, sometimes until the researcher came back. But what interested Mischel most was not only who waited. It was how they did it.

show.where: Bing Nursery School, Stanford University, late 1960s and early 1970s
show.what: Preschool children could eat one treat right away, or wait alone for the researcher to return and receive a larger reward.

segments.say: The children invented all kinds of clever strategies. Some turned their backs to the treat, or covered their eyes. Some sang quietly to themselves. Some played with their toes as if they were piano keys. Some invented little games. Some whispered reminders to themselves. If I wait, I get two. If I don't, I get one.

Isn't that lovely? Those little children discovered, all by themselves, many of the same strategies we've been talking about tonight. Move your attention away from what you're waiting for. Keep yourself occupied. Give your mind something else to do. The children who stared at the marshmallow found it much harder.

Mischel and his colleagues also found that how children thought about the treat made a big difference. When children focused on what researchers called the hot qualities, how sweet, chewy and yummy the marshmallow was, they tended to ring the bell sooner. When they focused on cool, abstract qualities, like how puffy and round it was, like a cotton ball, they could wait longer.

And one idea was especially clever. Some children were encouraged to imagine the treat as just a picture. To put a frame around it in their head. According to Stanford's own account of the research, children who did this waited much longer, almost eighteen minutes. As one child explained, well, you can't eat a picture.

This might be the most important lesson of the original marshmallow studies. Waiting isn't just about having or not having willpower. It's about strategy. About where you put your attention, and how you think about what you're waiting for. And strategies can be learned. Even by four year olds.

But the marshmallow test became famous for another reason. Years later, Mischel and his colleagues followed up some of the children, as teenagers and adults. And they reported that children who had waited longer tended, on average, to have better outcomes later. Better school results, for example, and some other positive measures.

This became a very powerful story. It was told in books, articles and talks around the world. A simple test with a marshmallow, at age four, seemed to predict success in life. Many people concluded that self control, measured in early childhood, was one of the most important ingredients for a good future.

But as we learned in our video about the brain's lies, a powerful story isn't the same as a complete truth. The original follow up groups were relatively small, and most of the children came from a university community. So in later years, other researchers wanted to test the idea with bigger, more varied groups of children. And what they found added some important nuance.

Before we get to that, let's hold on to the warm part of this story. Small children, alone in a room with a treat, singing songs, covering their eyes, turning marshmallows into pictures. They were figuring out, with great creativity, how to wait for something they wanted. In a way, all of us are still doing the same thing, just with bigger marshmallows.

So here's what those children taught us. Looking away from what you want makes waiting easier. Keeping busy, even with a song or a game, helps the time pass. Thinking about things in a cool, abstract way reduces temptation. And waiting is a skill that can be learned.

show.title: What the children taught us
items: Keeping busy helps the time pass
Thinking cool, not hot, reduces temptation
Waiting is a skill that can be learned

segments.say: So, did waiting for a marshmallow really predict a child's future? Next, let's look at what later research found. Including one beautiful experiment showing that a child's decision to wait may depend a lot on something we haven't talked about yet. Trust.
